questions.question_text: Which is a valid int literal?
questions.explanation: 42 is an integer literal. 3.14 is a double, "7" is a String, and true is a boolean.

questions.question_text: What is 17 / 5 in Java?
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero: 17 / 5 = 3 (the remainder is discarded). Use a double operand for a decimal result.

questions.question_text: After int a = 7, b = 2; what is a / b * 2.0?
questions.explanation: a / b is integer division = 3, then 3 * 2.0 = 6.0. The integer division happens first, before the double multiplication.

questions.question_text: "hello".length() returns:
questions.explanation: length() counts characters: h-e-l-l-o = 5. Note length() is a method for Strings (with parentheses), while arrays use length without them.

questions.question_text: Math.sqrt(81) returns:
questions.explanation: Math.sqrt returns a double: √81 = 9.0. It always returns a double even for perfect squares.

questions.question_text: What does "Hello World".indexOf("o") return?
questions.explanation: indexOf returns the index of the FIRST occurrence: 'o' first appears at index 4 (H0 e1 l2 l3 o4). The second 'o' (index 7) is ignored.

questions.question_text: What prints? int n = 0; if (n != 0 && 10 / n > 1) System.out.print("yes"); else System.out.print("no");
questions.explanation: Short-circuit evaluation: n != 0 is false, so the second operand (10/n) is never evaluated, avoiding division by zero. Prints 'no'.

questions.question_text: The logical OR operator in Java is:
questions.explanation: || is logical OR (true if either operand is true). && is AND, ! is NOT, == is equality comparison.

questions.question_text: What does this print? int i = 1; while (i < 100) i *= 2; System.out.println(i);
questions.explanation: i doubles: 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128. At 64 the condition 64<100 is true, so it becomes 128; then 128<100 is false, printing 128.

questions.question_text: What does this build? String s = ""; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) s += i; System.out.println(s);
questions.explanation: Since s is a String, += concatenates: "1"+"2"+"3"+"4" = "1234". String concatenation, not addition, builds the result.

questions.question_text: A while loop checks its condition:
questions.option_b: before each iteration (may run zero times)
questions.explanation: A while loop tests the condition before each iteration, so it may run zero times. A do-while checks after, guaranteeing at least one run.

questions.question_text: An accessor (getter) method typically:
questions.option_b: returns the value of a private field
questions.explanation: Accessors return field values (e.g., getName()); mutators (setters) change them. Getters provide controlled read access to private data.

questions.question_text: What does the toString() method conventionally do?
questions.option_b: return a String representation of the object, used when printing
questions.explanation: Overriding toString() defines how an object prints (System.out.println(obj) calls it). The default returns a class name and hash code.

questions.question_text: What does this print? int[] a = {10, 20, 30}; a[1] = a[0] + a[2]; System.out.println(a[1]);
questions.explanation: a[0] + a[2] = 10 + 30 = 40, assigned to a[1]. The element at index 1 becomes 40.

questions.question_text: What does this count? int[] a={2,5,8,3,6}; int c=0; for(int v:a) if(v%2==0) c++;
questions.explanation: Counts even values: 2, 8, 6 are even → c = 3. The condition v%2==0 selects even numbers.

questions.question_text: Arrays in Java have a fixed:
questions.explanation: An array's length is fixed when created and cannot change. To resize, you create a new array (or use an ArrayList).

questions.question_text: What does list.size() return for an empty ArrayList?
questions.explanation: An empty ArrayList has size 0. size() returns the current number of elements, growing as you add.

questions.question_text: After list = [1,2,3,4], what is list after list.remove(1)?
questions.explanation: remove(1) with an int removes the element at INDEX 1 (the value 2), giving [1, 3, 4]. Indices shift down after removal.

questions.question_text: To loop through all elements of a 2D array, you typically use:
questions.option_b: nested loops (one for rows, one for columns)
questions.explanation: Nested loops traverse a 2D array: the outer loop iterates rows, the inner loop iterates columns. This visits every element systematically.

questions.question_text: For int[][] g = new int[3][5], what is g[2].length?
questions.explanation: g[2] is a row with 5 columns, so g[2].length = 5. g.length is the number of rows (3); g[row].length is the columns.

questions.question_text: The keyword 'super' is used to:
questions.option_b: call the superclass's constructor or methods
questions.explanation: super invokes the parent class's constructor (super(...)) or its methods (super.method()). It lets a subclass reuse parent behavior.

questions.question_text: If Dog extends Animal, which assignment is valid?
questions.explanation: A subclass object can be assigned to a superclass reference (Animal a = new Dog()) — upcasting is always safe. The reverse (Dog d = new Animal()) needs an explicit, possibly unsafe cast.

questions.question_text: What does sum(4) return? int sum(int n){ if(n==0) return 0; return n + sum(n-1);}
questions.explanation: Sums 4+3+2+1+0 = 10. Each call adds n to the sum of all smaller numbers, with base case sum(0)=0.

questions.question_text: What is the base case in a recursive method?
questions.option_b: the condition that stops recursion without calling itself
questions.explanation: The base case ends recursion by returning without a further recursive call, preventing infinite recursion. Every recursive method needs at least one.

questions.question_text: Which compound assignment doubles x?
questions.explanation: x *= 2 multiplies x by 2 (doubles it). x += 2 adds 2; x /= 2 halves; x -= 2 subtracts 2.

questions.question_text: De Morgan's law states !(a && b) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: By De Morgan's law, !(a && b) = !a || !b. Negating an AND gives an OR of the negations (and vice versa).

questions.question_text: Encapsulation in OOP is achieved primarily by:
questions.option_b: making fields private and providing public methods to access them
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides data with private fields and exposes controlled access via public methods, protecting object integrity. It's a core OOP principle.

questions.question_text: Which method retrieves the element at index i in an ArrayList?
questions.explanation: ArrayLists use get(i) to retrieve elements (not bracket notation, which is for arrays). set(i, val) replaces an element.

questions.question_text: Polymorphism allows a single method call to:
questions.option_b: behave differently depending on the actual object type
questions.explanation: Polymorphism lets the same call (a.makeSound()) execute the appropriate overridden version based on the runtime object. It enables flexible, extensible code.
